More fun facts comparing flu rate to SARS-CoV-2 rate:

During the 2019-2020 flu season, the peak week experienced around 21,260 new confirmed cases of influenza[1].

During the most-recent week for which we have influenza data from the CDC, "week 11," there were

  • 6297 new confirmed influenza cases [2]
  • 2981 new confirmed SARS-CoV-2 cases [3]

During "week 12," we don't have an influenza count from the CDC yet, but the US reported

  • 29,800 new SARS-CoV-2 cases [3]

During the last 7 days (straddling "week 12" and "week 13" per the CDC's flu data), the US reported

  • 58,000 new SARS-CoV-2 cases [3]

58,000 new SARS-CoV-2 cases in the last 7 days is already 2.7x the peak weekly prevalence of new influenza infections (and over 9 times the most recently-reported week of new influenza infections). It would need to be peaking today and 2.7x less-severe than influenza for the net effect on society to be felt as mildly as the seasonal flu.

Of course, one should wonder what we'd find for influenza if we tested every member of the population or at least tested at the scale we're testing for SARS-CoV-2. Anecdotally (though assuredly not always), a negative influenza test is a precursor to a SARS-CoV-2 test so it's probably safe to assume that there's a spike in influenza testing that matches the movement of, if not the exact quantity of, the SARS-CoV-2 tests.

At some point, SARS-CoV-2 testing will surpass the rate of influenza testing, and then we might expect that we're detecting more of the SARS-CoV-2 cases in the population, proportionally, than we're detecting influenza cases. Until the SARS-CoV-2 confirmed deaths surpasses the maximum estimated influenza deaths (59,000 estimated for the 2019-2020 flu season [4]), someone will always be able to argue that we're just finding more SARS-CoV-2 cases because we're looking harder.
